progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C13 (NAGSAG with exceptions; list the ions, swap partners, check both; precipitate, spectator ions; net ionic equations; "no precipitate", not "no reaction"; after filtering, the solution holds the spectators plus any ion in excess; AgCl white, PbI2 bright yellow, BaSO4 white), C11 (dissolved ionic compounds are separate hydrated ions), Year 11 (ionic formulas, variables, risk assessment). P01 introduced validity, reliability and accuracy in plain words, but P01 is a branch, so this video gives the plain meanings again in one line each.
progression.startsWith: Controlled ionic-solution tests supply primary observations. The video opens: Twenty-five tiny wells. Five positive ions down the side, five negative ions across the top, and a few drops of each in every well.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why the cations are supplied as nitrates and the anions as sodium salts; planning the microscale matrix with predictions first, a check of each stock alone, a clean dropper technique and a black background; naming the independent, dependent and controlled variables and why concentration matters; stating the expected results and tracing each to a rule; writing a rule as a general statement with evidence and exceptions, and separating untested rules; classifying a mismatch as a wrong rule or a technique problem; testing the liquid above a precipitate to find the ion in excess; defining validity, reliability and accuracy for this investigation; writing a risk assessment for lead, silver, barium and hydroxide solutions. No Ksp, no Qsp, no conduct.
progression.nextLesson: Ksp, a number for how slightly soluble a compound is (route chem-m5-c14).

teaching.task: How do you set up a solubility investigation so a solid can only mean one thing, and how do you turn a grid of results into rules and test your predictions?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the grid is the evidence the rules come from (1); (2) nitrates and sodium salts always dissolve, so the only possible solid in a well is the pair being tested; each stock is checked alone first (2); (3) predicting first turns the results into a test; microscale method; keep the dropper out of the well; black background shows white solids (3); (4) variables, and why concentration matters most (4); (5) expected results, each traceable to NAGSAG (5); (6) rows and columns become rules, each with evidence and exceptions; untested ions are not your conclusion (6); (7) a mismatch is either a wrong rule or a technique problem; slightly soluble is a real third category; repeat doubtful cells (7); (8) testing the liquid above a precipitate shows which ion was left over (8); (9) validity, reliability, accuracy for this investigation (9); (10) risk assessment (10); memory aids (11); two attempts with brief feedback (12 to 15); decision rule and handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: the investigation is a test of predictions. Design for validity (always-soluble partners, a check of each stock alone), predict every cell, mix microscale, record carefully, read patterns into rules with evidence, evaluate every mismatch, then analyse a mixture's composition by testing its liquid. Validity, reliability and accuracy are named on this investigation. Risk assessment with the real hazards.
teaching.openingDecision: This grid is the evidence the solubility rules come from. So how do you set it up so the results can be trusted, and how do you turn a grid of cloudy wells into rules?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1, Revision 2) potassium chloride mixed with silver nitrate (a syllabus pair); the white solid settles; a drop of potassium chloride added to the clear liquid above gives more white solid: which ions were in that liquid? Answer: K+, NO3- and leftover Ag+ (silver nitrate was in excess). Crossed mistake: "chloride ions left over". This transfers the scene 8 logic to a new system and the opposite reagent role; it also differs from C13's attempt 2 (chloride in excess, filtrate named from the excess). (A2) two groups mix calcium nitrate with sodium sulfate; one sees a faint white cloud, the other nothing: explain both, and how to make the result more reliable. Answer: CaSO4 slightly soluble, so whether a cloud shows depends on the amounts (drop size, concentration) and waiting time; a dirty well can fake a cloud; repeat in clean wells with the same concentrations, drops and waiting time, over black, and record "slight". Crossed mistake: "one group was just wrong".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (2017, p51, C5-IQ4-03): "conduct an investigation to determine solubility rules, and predict and analyse the composition of substances when two ionic solutions are mixed, for example: potassium chloride and silver nitrate; potassium iodide and lead nitrate; sodium sulfate and barium nitrate (ACSCH065)". This video prepares students to plan, record and analyse the investigation and does not claim to replace conducting it.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer, three constant zones (short question top left, apparatus centre, one current card in the right third). Colour key: positive ions amber, negative ions violet, every precipitate in its real colour, spectators grey, predictions in pen, observations as the wells themselves. Reuse and new items: C13's rules card (small, scene 5), the C13 matrix grid style (now drawn as wells), the C13 swap-cross icon (scene 2, small), the C13 equation strip for the PbI2 net equation (scene 8), the C13 composition card ("solid / dissolved"), `m5x-ppt-pbi2-yellow-v1.png` (settled yellow solid with clear liquid above; scene 8), `m5x-ppt-agcl-white-v1.png` (attempt 1, Revision 2), `m5x-ppt-agcl-white-v1.png`, `m5x-no-ppt-clear-v1.png`, `m5x-ppt-baso4-white-v1.png` (requested in the C13 brief; interim as C13), `m5x-graduated-pipette-v1.png` (drawing off the clear liquid), `m6-white-tile-v1.png`, `m6-wash-bottle-v1.png`, the P01 shared safety plates (`m5x-safety-glasses-v1.png`, `m5x-gloves-v1.png`, `m5x-waste-bottle-v1.png`) and `m5x-dropper-clear-v1.png` (P01 Codex items 5, 9 to 11), the countdown ring and the key notes board. New coded items: the well fills (drops landing, clear, cloud, solid in its real colour), the predict-then-observe overlay (each cell shows the prediction as a pen mark and the observation as the well), the black card under the plate (a plain rectangle), the rule-with-evidence card, the mismatch sorter ("rule wrong" / "technique"), the variables card, the risk table. New painted plates are listed in the Codex asset brief (well plate, dropper bottle).
